Riyadh rocked by explosions as Iranian strikes in Hormuz rise

Saudi Arabia’s capital came under intense attack from the Houthis on Monday night local time after the Yemeni group claimed it targeted Riyadh’s airport, following repeated strikes on the city over the weekend.

Yemen’s Houthis said on Monday that they targeted the airport with a ballistic missile and also claimed to have targeted King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait.

One western official in Riyadh confirmed to Middle East Eye multiple blasts and explosions across the capital, as video footage on social media appeared to show raging fires. MEE could not independently confirm the video.

The strikes underscore a widening of the war in Yemen and pose a serious challenge to Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions.

The Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia come against the backdrop of rising tensions in the Middle East, with the region facing the potential of a return to US-Israeli attacks on Iran.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Monday that they attacked a supertanker in the Strait of Hormuz trying to leave the waterway. The strike would mark the third attack on vessels in two days.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] The resilience of the world economy is built on illusion - it's time the West woke up
item.description:
The resilience of the world economy is built on illusion - it's time the West woke up

Submitted by Marco Carnelos on Sun, 10/11/2026 - 15:30
Record debt, a paralysed trade-dispute architecture and the normalisation of sovereign-asset seizure as a policy tool means fragility is baked into the global economic system
In his Davos speech this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney recognised that powerful nations were using economic coercion to get what they want, pictured in Alberta, Canada, 1 October 2026 (Reuters/Todd Korol)
Off

Since 2022, a steady drumbeat of forecasts has warned that cascading military and political upheavals - war in Ukraine, conflict in the Middle East, an accelerating tariff war, the weaponisation of sanctions and the disruption of energy supplies - would eventually overwhelm the world economy’s capacity to absorb shocks. 

The most destructive of those scenarios have not materialised, or at least not yet.

As the IMF's managing director Kristalina Georgieva stated last year, while previewing the fund's World Economic Outlook, the global economy "has generally withstood significant strains from various shocks". 

Although that resilience is real, on closer inspection, it is a more fragile and more contested achievement than it first appears.

The adaptive mechanisms behind this resilience are visible and measurable. Trade has rerouted rather than collapsed. Energy corridors have diversified. And reserve managers have spent the past three years quietly re-engineering the architecture of the international monetary system. 

According to the World Gold Council's 2026 Central Bank Gold Reserves survey - which drew responses from 76 institutions, its highest participation in nine years - 89 percent of central banks expect global gold holdings to keep rising over the next year, with a record share planning to add to their own reserves. 

The result: gold has overtaken US Treasuries as the largest single component of global central bank reserves for the first time since the mid-1990s.

Mother of all ticking bombs 

Analysts tracking the shift link it directly to a single event: reserve managers were unsettled by the seizure of the Central Bank of Russia's reserves at the start of the Ukraine war by Washington and have since been actively reducing the dollar share of their portfolios. 

Debt of this scale narrows the fiscal space available to absorb the next shock, military or otherwise, which is precisely what makes today's resilience difficult to extrapolate into tomorrow's

This is a clear example that the economic system is not breaking under political pressure, it is adapting to it - flexibly, and crucially, without severing the interconnections that make global trade and finance function at all. 

In other words, central banks accumulating gold are not exiting the system; they are just hedging within it.

But adaptability has a cost, and that cost is compounding.

Global debt - government, household, corporate and financial combined - surpassed $365 trillion in the first half of 2026, according to the Institute of International Finance's Global Debt Monitor, the sixth consecutive quarterly record. 

Emerging-market debt alone rose by $6.5 trillion in the same period, breaking past $110 trillion. Georgieva has been blunt about the trajectory: speaking at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, she warned that global public debt is projected to reach 110 percent of the world's GDP by 2029.

There is an evident reluctance to address what is not a crisis in any single country's balance sheet, but a structural drift that every major economy appears aware of and none is prepared to correct unilaterally. 

Debt of this scale narrows the fiscal space available to absorb the next shock, military or otherwise, which is precisely what makes today's resilience difficult to extrapolate into tomorrow's.

In this context, there is also the mother of all ticking bombs, a nuclear one: the $40 trillion US federal debt which US Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent is desperately trying to reign in.

The third strand, the onslaught of punitive political measures targeting market principles, is best illustrated by the fate of Russia's frozen central bank reserves. Roughly $300bn in Russian sovereign assets have been immobilised globally since 2022, with some €210bn ($235bn) held within the European Union.

Erosion of neutrality

Rather than remaining in legal limbo, these reserves have become the financial engine of a specific policy outcome: the EU's proposed €140bn ($157bn) "reparations loan" to Ukraine, structured so that Ukraine would repay it only once Russia itself pays war damages - effectively converting a sanctions freeze into a grant.

Russia's central bank has responded by suing the Brussels-based depository Euroclear, which holds the bulk of the assets, calling the manoeuvre illegal.

Whatever one's view of the underlying conflict, the precedent is the point economists increasingly raise: the first large-scale use of frozen sovereign reserves as collateral for a geopolitical objective changes the calculus for every reserve-holding state watching from outside the western bloc.

It is one more data pointing to the reinforcing of the gold-accumulation trend described above - and a vivid example of how political tools aimed at a single adversary can erode the perceived neutrality of the system itself.

A parallel erosion is under way in trade governance. The WTO's Appellate Body (the one supposed to settle trade dispute among countries) has been non-functional since December 2019, after the United States blocked the appointment of new judges and talks on reviving or replacing it remain stuck.

More than 30 appeals currently sit unresolved, and the workaround mechanism created to fill the gap - the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement - has resolved only a single case. The institution designed to prevent trade disputes from becoming purely a function of relative power has been quietly sidelined for seven years.

It is then worth wondering - in such a situation - if the Global West and Global Rest see the same picture here.

The evidence suggests convergence on diagnosis but real divergence on meaning. Both recognise that debt is unsustainable and that institutions are strained. But where western policymakers tend to treat sanctions, frozen assets and trade paralysis as defensive responses to external aggression.

Voices from the Global Rest increasingly read the same tools as confirmation that the system was never as neutral as advertised.

India's External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar captured this gap memorably in 2022, telling European interlocutors that Europe needed to "grow out of the mindset" that its problems are everyone's problems while the reverse does not hold. 

Selective status

This is something many Global Rest governments had been thinking but not saying aloud: that the postwar order's claim to universality was always, in practice, more selective than it appeared.

Why the EU's sanctions on Sudan's gold trade are fundamentally flawed
Read More »

The more honest and outspoken western leader to recognise such an unfair situation, to use an understatement, was Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier this year in Davos.

None of this means the system is about to fracture. The world economy has proven more elastic than feared, absorbing shocks that a decade ago might have triggered genuine crisis. But elasticity and durability are not the same thing. 

The real test of this sort of "economy of resistance" is not whether it survives the next military-political storm - it plainly has, repeatedly.

It is whether record debt, a paralysed trade-dispute architecture, and the normalisation of sovereign-asset seizures as a policy tool are quietly converting what is in effect a short-term adaptability into long-term fragility, especially at a moment when the Global Rest and Global West can no longer agree on what the system is actually for.
